analysis.one_liner: Lets student borrowers wipe out their student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill to let student borrowers erase their loans in bankruptcy died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, student loans are almost the only kind of debt you cannot erase in bankruptcy — credit cards and medical bills can be discharged, but student loans follow you unless you prove 'undue hardship,' a standard most borrowers cannot meet. This bill would strike that special rule from federal bankruptcy law, letting student loans be wiped out in bankruptcy like any other debt. It never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the entire two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers who fall into serious financial distress — job loss, illness, disability — would gain a genuine way out. Under current law they must sue in bankruptcy court and prove 'undue hardship,' a test so strict that most never bother to try.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the special bankruptcy exception for student loans, letting borrowers who file for bankruptcy treat these loans like credit card or medical debt — discharged when they cannot pay.
It covers all student loan types: government, nonprofit, and private, plus repayment obligations for educational benefits and scholarships.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and the federal government would absorb losses when borrowers discharge loans, and those costs could be passed on as somewhat higher interest rates or tighter lending for future students.
analysis.who_pays_short: Loan issuers and federal loan program

drawbacks.text: Allowing bankruptcy discharge would expose the federal government and private lenders to losses on loans made to borrowers who later file for bankruptcy, which could push up interest rates on student loans for all borrowers.
The change applies only to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, so it offers no relief to borrowers already trapped in old loans unless they can sustain a new filing years later.

Because bankruptcy becomes a realistic exit, critics worry some borrowers might time filings strategically, and lenders would tighten underwriting, potentially limiting access to loans for students with thin credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For struggling borrowers, the benefit is substantial: a genuine exit from debt that currently follows them for life. The main costs and risks are real but manageable: interest rates on student loans could rise to reflect the added risk of discharge, some borrowers might pay more, and lenders would face higher losses. Most other consumer debts have been dischargeable for decades without collapsing those credit markets. The bill was so narrow and modestly written that its death appears attributable to lack of congressional action rather than a weighed tradeoff.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee never acted on it, so it never came to a vote in the House or Senate and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 24, 2019 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law in March 2019 and never advanced further.
No committee vote, no House floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders, debt collectors, and the federal loan program keep the current rule that student debt is nearly impossible to escape, while borrowers who need bankruptcy relief are left with no option.

for.name: Rep. John Katko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.

for.name: Reps. Debbie Dingell and Alan Lowenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the entire Congress.

against.name: Higher education and lending interests
against.what_they_did: Long opposed loosening the bankruptcy discharge rule for student loans, arguing it would raise borrowing costs and invite abuse.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship — a Republican led it with 16 Democratic cosponsors — but no vote ever occurred, so party lines were never tested; the main fact is that the House leadership and Judiciary Committee gave it no floor time.

industries.note: Their loans become dischargeable, meaning they can no longer count on collecting from borrowers no matter how dire the borrower's finances. This restores risk to a market that had been largely risk-free for lenders.
The federal Direct Loan program loses its guarantee that education debt is nearly always repaid, absorbing losses when borrowers discharge in bankruptcy. The program's cost of lending would rise.
Student loan debt becomes harder to pursue against bankrupt borrowers, shrinking the collection business built on the current no-escape rule.
